text: Shift Supervisor, System Operations
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Twenty-two years on the desk, eleven of them on nights. She runs the room
the way a bridge is run: nobody touches a control without saying out loud
what they expect to happen, and then whether it did.

Her rule is that frequency is the only number on the wall that belongs to
everybody. Voltage is local and can be argued about; frequency is the whole
interconnection agreeing or failing to agree, and it moves before anything
else does.

Her limit is that she is paid to act before the picture is complete. The
operator who waits for certainty is the operator who watches the cascade.

text: Generation Lead
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Came up through turbine commissioning and still walks a machine hall
listening rather than reading. She can tell a governor hunting from the
sound of it before the trend on the screen has moved.

What she wants understood is that a generator is a flywheel first and a
power source second. The stored rotational energy is what buys the seconds
in which anybody gets to make a decision.

Her limit is ramp rate. A machine that can supply four hundred megawatts
cannot supply them in the ninety seconds after a trip, and no amount of
wanting changes the thermal gradient in a steam drum.

text: Protection Engineer
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Sets the relays, which means he designs the conditions under which the
network is allowed to give up on part of itself. He describes the job as
writing the rules for an argument that will happen in eighty milliseconds
with nobody present.

A relay that never trips is not a cautious relay, it is a relay that lets a
fault burn. A relay that trips early takes out a healthy line and moves the
overload somewhere less convenient. Coordination is the whole discipline.

His limit is that he is protecting against faults he has to imagine in
advance, and the cascade always finds the sequence nobody drew.

text:
Runs the feeders, which is where the network acquires customers, trees and
opinions. She points out that every elegant thing decided in the control
room arrives here as a van, a pole and somebody's evening.

Her measure of a restoration is not megawatts, it is households and how
long they waited, and she will say so in a meeting about megawatts.

Her limit is that the low-voltage network is only sparsely instrumented.
Past the substation she is often reasoning from the shape of the load
rather than from a reading.

text: Load Forecasting
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Forecasts demand, which he insists is a branch of anthropology conducted
with a thermometer. Weather, the television schedule, the school holidays
and whether it gets dark before people get home.

He is precise about what a forecast is: a distribution, not a number. The
useful output is the width, because the width is what the reserve has to
cover.

His limit is that the events worth forecasting are rare by construction, so
the model is always best calibrated for the days that matter least.

note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Owns the question nobody wants to open during an incident: is that number
the number. Instrument transformers, telemetry lag, clock skew, and the
cheerful confidence of a meter reading the wrong side of a saturated core.

She keeps the traceability chain because after the event there will be an
inquiry, and the inquiry will run on the records rather than on anybody's
memory of the night.

Her limit is that she is usually reconstructing rather than observing, and
the highest-value seconds are the ones with the worst data.

text: Tuesday, 04:12, and the largest unit on the Calder system has tripped without warning. Frequency fell and then steadied somewhere below where it began, which Dolores Reyes says matters more than the fall itself — a system that stops falling has found a new balance, and the new balance is short. Nadia Haddad has machines that can make up the shortfall but not in the next two minutes. June Farrow wants the records checked before anybody calls it a lost unit, and Reyes is not waiting: a system this far short does not get more certain while you read about it. This morning Reyes is right. Today you read what the frequency is telling you, work out how much generation actually went missing, and decide what to ask for first. Read it as a fault on one machine and you will spend the morning fixing the wrong thing.

text: Frequency is set by the balance between what the machines generate and what the customers draw, everywhere at once. That is because every synchronous machine on the system turns in step. So a fall means demand now exceeds generation. The rate of the fall measures the size of the mismatch against the spinning inertia that was there to absorb it. Flattening is not recovery. The governors have found a new equilibrium at a lower speed, and it will stay there until something adds real power. Voltage tells you where the problem is. Frequency tells you that there is one, and how large.

text: In the first instant after a trip nothing has responded yet. No governor, no reserve. The only thing opposing the imbalance is the rotational energy already spinning. That gives the swing relation: the rate of frequency change equals the power imbalance divided by twice the stored inertia, in the same units. Rearranged, the imbalance is the rate of change times twice the inertia, times the nominal frequency to get back to megawatts. It is the cleanest measurement the first two seconds offer, and it arrives before any telemetry from the tripped plant.

text: A record carries two different claims and they fail independently. The absolute timestamp says when, and it is only as good as the clock that stamped it. The intervals between a record's own entries say in what order and how far apart. Those survive a drifting clock intact. Here the relay's intervals agree with the GPS-locked recorder while its absolute time does not, which is exactly the signature of drift rather than of an early operation. The SCADA scan is not wrong either — it is simply too slow to order anything inside a four-second window, and treating its two samples as a sequence is how an inquiry invents a cause.

text: A conductor's rating is a thermal limit reached over time. So the first move is to establish how much time there is: the emergency rating, and the minutes it is good for. Then the cheapest reversible action, which is to redispatch generation so less flow takes that path. Reconfiguring the network comes next, because switching changes what the remaining contingencies are and cannot be undone in seconds. Shedding load is last. Not because it is drastic, but because it is the only step that takes the decision away from customers, and every earlier step that works makes it unnecessary. In the wrong order, an operator sheds load to protect a line that could have been unloaded by moving two hundred megawatts.

text: Both circuits start and finish at the same two busbars, so the voltage across each is identical. By Ohm's law the current in each is that voltage divided by its own impedance, which means the smaller impedance carries the larger current. Working the shares out gives each path the other one's impedance over the sum. This is why adding a circuit does not split flow evenly, and why a new low-impedance line can quietly overload itself while an old one sits half empty. Nothing on the total meter shows any of it.

text: Two arrangements, and the thing that stays common is what tells them apart. End to end there is only one path, so every element passes the same current and the supply voltage divides between them in proportion to impedance. Side by side each element sees the whole voltage, so the current divides instead. Everything else follows. Adding a parallel branch lowers the combined impedance and raises the total current, while adding a series element raises the impedance and lowers it. Getting these the wrong way round is how somebody sizes a fuse for the wrong number.

text: Normal load current is set by what the customer is drawing. Fault current is not: the load has been bypassed, so the only thing left to limit the flow is the impedance of the source, the transformer and the cable back to it. That is a very small number, and dividing the phase voltage by it gives a current tens of times larger than anything the circuit carries in service. This is why switchgear is rated for a breaking current rather than a running one, and why the clearing time is quoted in milliseconds. The energy released goes as the current squared times the time.

text: How does the current transformer produce its reading?
note: the question itself

text: A current in a conductor makes a magnetic field around it. If the current alternates, the field alternates with it, and a changing field through a coil drives a voltage in that coil. That is Faraday's law, and it is the whole basis of the instrument: the two circuits share a magnetic path and no electrical one, which is what keeps the meter and the person reading it at low voltage. It is also why a current transformer works only on alternating current. On direct current the field is steady, nothing changes, and the reading is zero.

text: A load curve is the same shape most days, because people do the same things at the same times. What moves it is weather, and the useful form of that is a sensitivity: how many megawatts one degree is worth on this system, measured from this winter's own data rather than from a textbook. Base plus sensitivity times degrees gets the centre of the forecast. It does not get the width, which is what the reserve has to cover, and the width comes from how wrong the temperature forecast itself can be. Both numbers are needed and they answer different questions.

text: Dispatch starts from cost, because running the cheapest first is what makes electricity affordable. Then three things bend it. Plant with almost no running cost goes first and cannot be relied on, so it displaces fuel without displacing the need for something reliable behind it. Plant that can change output quickly is worth holding part-loaded, because reserve is a service and a machine at full output cannot provide it. And plant in the right place can be needed regardless of price, when the alternative is a corridor over its limit. None of these is charity. Each is the system paying for something other than energy.

text: Each store answers over a different interval and confusing them is how a plan fails. Rotational energy in a spinning machine is there instantly, without anybody asking, and it is gone in seconds. A battery through an inverter responds in well under a second and can hold for hours, which makes it the most useful thing an island can have. Energy in the magnetic fields of transformers and lines is real, and it is a fraction of a cycle: nothing dispatchable. Boiler thermal storage is minutes away, useful for the recovery and useless for the first ten seconds.
